turns.prompt_text: My apartment I have a lot of floor space and I have hardwood floors around the living area with the TV and the seating. I need a rug rugs are pretty expensive. I want a pretty large one. Could I DIY that somehow?
turns.response_html:
Creating a large rug for a big living area can definitely be a budget-saver, especially since commercial rugs in the 8'x10' or 9'x12' range can easily hit several hundred dollars. Since you have hardwood floors, a DIY approach also allows you to customize the backing to ensure it doesn’t slide or scratch the wood.

Here are a few ways you can DIY a large-scale rug, ranging from "no-sew" to more hands-on projects.

1. The Carpet Tile Mosaic

This is the most professional-looking DIY and is incredibly durable. You can often find discontinued carpet tiles or "remnants" at flooring outlets for a fraction of the price of a rug.

  • How to do it: Purchase enough tiles to cover your area. Use carpet tape or specialized "dots" to join the tiles to each other from the underside.
  • The Benefit: If you spill something (like Tikka Masala), you only have to replace or deep-clean one tile instead of an entire 9-foot rug.

2. The Painted Drop Cloth Rug

If you want something massive and lightweight, heavy-duty canvas drop cloths (the kind painters use) are the secret weapon.

  • How to do it:
    1. Buy a large, heavyweight canvas drop cloth.
    2. Hem the edges using permanent fabric glue or a sewing machine.
    3. Paint your design using latex paint mixed with a fabric medium (this keeps the paint from cracking and keeps the rug flexible).
    4. Crucial Step: You must seal it with a water-based polyurethane to make it wipeable and durable.
  • The Vibe: This creates a flat-weave look similar to a "dhurrie" rug.

3. The Custom "Remnant" Bound Rug

Go to a local carpet warehouse or a "big box" home improvement store and look for remnants—these are the end-of-the-roll pieces left over from wall-to-wall installations.

  • How to do it: Buy a large remnant (often 70-80% off retail). To DIY the "finished" edge without a professional binding machine, you can use Instabind. It’s a DIY carpet binding tape that you simply stick to the edge and seal with a hot glue gun.
  • The Benefit: It looks exactly like a high-end store-bought rug but costs significantly less.

4. Rope or Jute Coil Rug

If you want a more organic, textured look, you can make a giant coil rug using sisal or jute rope.

  • How to do it: Start in the center and coil the rope tightly, using high-temp hot glue or a heavy-duty zig-zag stitch on a sewing machine to join the rounds.
  • Pro-Tip: For a rug this large, it’s easier to make several smaller circles and join them together into a "cluster" rug rather than trying to manhandle one giant 10-foot coil.

Important Considerations for Hardwood Floors

Since you are working with hardwood, the DIY rug itself is only half the battle. You’ll need to address protection and stability:

  • Non-Slip Padding: Always place a felt or rubberized rug pad underneath. DIY rugs (especially the drop cloth version) are very light and will slide dangerously on hardwood.
  • Adhesive Warning: Never use "carpet tape" directly on your hardwood; it can leave a residue that ruins the finish. Only use tape to join the rug materials to each other or to a rug pad.

turns.prompt_text: What are some of the stores that would carry these tiles these carpet tiles?
turns.response_html:
To find carpet tiles for your living area, you can look at both large national retailers and local flooring outlets near Ames and Ankeny. Because you are looking for a more affordable DIY option, focusing on stores that carry in-stock inventory or remnants will be your best bet.

National Retailers (Best for In-Stock & Peel-and-Stick)

These stores typically have dedicated flooring sections where you can find individual tiles or boxes ready for pickup.

  • Lowe's: The Ames location (Airport Rd) stocks a variety of carpet tiles, including Style Selections and TrafficMaster. They are a great place to see the texture in person before committing to a large quantity.
  • Menards: Known for having competitive pricing on bulk carpet tiles, they often carry commercial-grade options that are very durable for high-traffic TV areas.
  • Home Depot: They carry a wide range of peel-and-stick tiles that are specifically designed for easy DIY installation without needing separate adhesives.
  • Target: While they don't have as much "in-store" flooring as hardware shops, they carry brands like Foss Floors online with fast shipping, which are popular for their modern, low-profile designs.

Specialized & Design-Forward Options

If you want something that looks less like "office carpet" and more like a high-end rug, consider these:

  • FLOR: They specialize in designer carpet tiles meant specifically to be used as area rugs. Styles like Rush Street or Parallel Reality offer unique patterns and textures that don't always require a full-room installation to look good.

Local Flooring Outlets (Best for Budget/Remnants)

For the most significant savings, you can check local outlets that sell discontinued lines or remnants:

  • Carpet One Floor & Home (Ames): Located on South Duff Avenue, they often have a larger variety of textures than big-box stores and may have remnants from larger commercial jobs.
  • Flooring America (Ankeny): Since you are often in Ankeny, this is a convenient spot to check for clearance tiles or overstock from residential projects.

Shopping Tips for Your Hardwood Floors

  • Check the Backing: Look for tiles with a bitumen or rubber backing; these stay in place better on hardwood than thin felt-backed tiles.
  • Dye Lots: If you buy from an outlet or "remnant" section, ensure all boxes have the same dye lot number so the colors match perfectly across your living area.
  • Quantity: For a large rug (like an 8'x10'), you'll need roughly 20-25 tiles if they are the standard 24"x24" size.
